note: 内置经典轻奇幻示范作品：海边小镇的灯塔在沉寂七年后重新亮起，制图师 Mara 循着地图上的名字找回小镇遗忘的约定。
title: The Lantern Keeper
synopsis: When a silent lighthouse begins sending messages to an empty sea, a young mapmaker discovers that her quiet town has forgotten something important.
bible: Mara is a practical adult mapmaker. Elian is an elderly lighthouse keeper. Setting: the coastal town of Bellweather. Gentle fantasy. Third-person past tense. The lighthouse preserves memories of people lost at sea. No resurrection; remembering allows the town to grieve.
outline: Mara sees a light and finds an old map.
The keeper reveals a forgotten promise.
Mara returns the names to the town and the light rests.
sample: The lighthouse had been dark for seven years. On Tuesday evening, it began to shine again. Mara noticed it from the window of her little map shop. The light moved across the water, slowly and carefully, as if someone were searching for a lost key.
memory: Complete: the names are restored to the town map and a harbour sign. Elian shares his memories. The lighthouse goes dark peacefully.

preset.preferences: A gentle mystery in a coastal town.

chapters.title: 1 · A Light Across the Water
chapters.summary: Mara notices the lighthouse and discovers a hidden list of names on an old map.
chapters.memory: Mara saw the light. An old map contains three names: Ada, Tomas, and June. She will visit Elian.
chapters.text:
The lighthouse had been dark for seven years. On Tuesday evening, it began to shine again.

Mara noticed it from the window of her little map shop. The light moved across the water, slowly and carefully, as if someone were searching for a lost key. It passed the fishing boats. It passed the stone wall. Then it stopped on her window.

She put down her pencil.

“That is strange,” she said to the empty room.

Outside, rain was drawing thin lines on the glass. The street smelled of salt and wet wood. Most of the shops had already closed, but a warm light still shone from the bakery across the road.

Mara opened her door. “Did you see that?” she called to the baker.

“See what?” he asked.

“The lighthouse.”

The baker looked towards the hill. The tower stood dark against the evening sky.

“Nothing there,” he said gently. “Perhaps you have been working too long.”

Mara did not argue. She went inside and checked the window. On the table below it lay a map she had bought that morning. It was a map of Bellweather, but some of its streets had different names. The harbour was smaller. The lighthouse was marked with a tiny golden star.

Now, where the light had touched the paper, three names were visible. Ada. Tomas. June.

She ran her finger beside them. The ink was dry, and the paper felt ordinary. Yet she was certain the names had not been there before.

Mara found her coat. At the door, she paused to take the map. There was only one person in town who still had a key to the lighthouse, and she knew where he lived.

The light appeared once more as she stepped into the rain. This time, it seemed almost patient.

chapters.title: 2 · The Keeper’s Promise
chapters.summary: Elian explains the light remembers three people lost at sea, whose names faded from public memory.
chapters.memory: Elian promised to keep Ada, Tomas and June in memory. The lighthouse needs their names restored publicly. Mara will inscribe them on her town map.
chapters.text:
Elian lived at the top of a steep street, in a house with blue steps. When Mara knocked, he opened the door before she could knock again.

“I wondered when you would come,” he said.

She held up the map. “Then you know about these names.”

Elian stepped aside. His kitchen was small and warm. A kettle waited on the stove. On the wall hung a photograph of three people standing beside a fishing boat.

“Ada was my sister,” he said. “Tomas was her husband. June was their friend. They sailed out during the winter storm, twenty years ago. They were trying to help another boat.”

Mara looked at the photograph. Ada was laughing. June had one hand raised against the sun.

“Did they come back?”

“No.” Elian poured the tea carefully. “For a long time, we spoke about them. We put flowers on the harbour wall. Then people moved away. Children grew up. The little sign with their names broke during a storm. I meant to repair it.”

He sat down. “But I did not.”

Mara waited. She had learned, through making maps, that empty spaces often needed time.

“The lighthouse was built to guide people home,” he continued. “But sometimes it keeps something else safe. A name. A promise. A thing we are not ready to lose.”

“Can it bring them back?” she asked.

Elian shook his head. “No light can do that.”

For a moment, there was only the sound of the kettle.

“Then what does it want?”

“Perhaps it wants us to remember together. I have been remembering alone for too long.”

Mara spread the map on the table. The three names seemed clearer here. She thought of the blank space beside the harbour on her new map, the one she was making for the town hall.

“I have an idea,” she said.

Elian looked at her, and for the first time that evening, he smiled.

chapters.title: 3 · A Place for Their Names
chapters.summary: Mara adds the names and story to the town map. The townspeople gather; the lighthouse rests.
chapters.memory: Complete: the names are restored to the town map and a harbour sign. Elian shares his memories. The lighthouse goes dark peacefully.
chapters.text:
On Saturday morning, Mara carried her new map to the town hall. Elian walked beside her. Under his arm, he held the photograph in a clean wooden frame.

The baker came out to watch them. “A new map?” he asked.

“An older story,” Mara replied.

They placed the map on the large table by the window. Mara had drawn the harbour in blue and gold. Beside it, in clear black letters, she had written three names. Below them was a short account of the winter storm and the boat that had sailed out to help.

People stopped to read. An old woman touched Ada’s name.

“She taught me to swim,” she said.

The baker looked at Tomas in the photograph. “My father spoke about him. He used to repair our door. I had forgotten his name.”

Soon, the room was full of small stories. Nobody knew everything. Together, they remembered enough.

Elian sat near the window and listened. Then he began to speak as well. He told them how his sister could never keep a plant alive, although she understood every kind of weather. He told them about June’s terrible singing. He laughed, and then he cried a little, and nobody asked him to stop.

That afternoon, the baker offered to make a new sign for the harbour wall. Mara promised to paint the letters.

As evening came, she walked home past the water. The lighthouse shone once. Its warm circle crossed the boats and rested on the town hall. Then the light grew smaller, until it was no brighter than a candle.

At last, it went out.

Mara stood still. This time, the dark tower did not feel empty.

The following morning, she opened her shop and found a new piece of paper. There were other maps to make. But first, she wrote three names at the top of a page, so she would always know where to begin.

note: 适合英语初级（CEFR A2）读者的温暖日常短篇：一张迟到十二年的明信片寄到了老钟表店，句式简短清晰。
title: The Clockmaker’s Postcard
synopsis: When a postcard from twelve years ago arrives at a quiet repair shop, a young apprentice sets out across the city to return a forgotten pocket watch.
bible: Noah is a careful twenty-four-year-old watch apprentice. Mrs. Linden is the former owner of the watch. Setting: an autumn city with trams and bookshops. Third-person past tense, warm slice of life.
outline: A late postcard arrives at the clock shop and points to a blue drawer.
Noah visits the old station café and learns where Mrs. Linden moved.
Noah returns the pocket watch at the riverside greenhouse.
sample: Every morning at eight, Noah opened the green shutters of the clock shop. On Thursday, the postman left a postcard on the counter. The picture showed a red tram in the rain, and the stamp was twelve years old.
memory: Noah returned the silver pocket watch to Mrs. Linden at the greenhouse, and it began ticking again.

preset.preferences: Short sentences, practical everyday vocabulary, warm adult characters.

chapters.title: 1 · The Blue Drawer
chapters.summary: Noah receives a twelve-year-old postcard and finds a silver pocket watch in a hidden drawer.
chapters.memory: Noah found watch number 47 and an address near the old station café.
chapters.text:
Every morning at eight, Noah opened the green shutters of the clock shop. The street outside was still quiet. A tram bell rang at the corner, and the smell of fresh bread came from the next door.

On Thursday, the postman put a small postcard on the wooden counter. “This one took a long time,” he said with a smile. “We found it behind an old sorting cabinet at the central office.”

Noah turned the card over. The picture showed a red tram in the rain. The stamp in the corner was twelve years old. Someone had written in neat blue ink: Please keep watch number 47 until Saturday. I will come after the noon train. — Clara Linden.

Noah worked with Mr. Hale, who had retired the previous month. Before leaving, Mr. Hale had told him, “Every drawer in this room has a story. Take your time with them.”

Noah walked to the back wall. Beneath the workbench stood a row of small blue drawers. He pulled open the one marked 40 to 50. Inside lay a silver pocket watch wrapped in soft grey cloth. Attached to the chain was a paper ticket with the number 47 and an address: 14 Station Lane.

He wound the crown gently. After a quiet pause, the watch began to tick. Its sound was steady and clear, as if twelve years had been only a short afternoon nap.

Noah looked at the clock on the wall. Today was his half-day off. He put the silver watch into a small leather box, slipped the postcard into his coat pocket, and locked the shop door behind him.

chapters.title: 2 · Tea by the Tracks
chapters.summary: At 14 Station Lane, a café owner helps Noah trace Clara Linden to the riverside greenhouse.
chapters.memory: Clara Linden now works at the municipal greenhouse by the river.
chapters.text:
Station Lane was only three stops away on the tram. The autumn wind blew yellow leaves along the pavement as Noah stepped down.

Number 14 was no longer an apartment building. Its ground floor had become a bright corner café with large windows and wooden tables. Inside, a woman in a brown apron was polishing glasses behind the counter.

“Good afternoon,” Noah said, holding up the old postcard. “I am looking for Clara Linden. She lived at this address twelve years ago.”

The woman wiped her hands and looked closely at the card. “Mrs. Linden! Of course I remember her. She lived upstairs before she moved to the quieter side of the river. She used to bring us fresh mint from her balcony.”

“Do you know where I can find her now?” Noah asked. “She left a watch at our shop a long time ago.”

“She volunteers at the riverside greenhouse every Thursday afternoon,” the café owner said. “Take the footpath past the stone bridge. You will see the glass roof among the willow trees.”

Before Noah left, she handed him a small paper bag with two warm cinnamon rolls. “Give one to Clara for me,” she said. “Tell her the station clock is still two minutes fast, just as she always complained.”

Noah thanked her and walked toward the river. The afternoon sun came through the clouds, turning the water a pale gold.

chapters.title: 3 · Time Kept Safe
chapters.summary: Noah meets Clara at the greenhouse and returns her late husband’s railway watch.
chapters.memory: Complete: Watch 47 is back with Clara Linden.
chapters.text:
The greenhouse stood beside the river like a quiet ship made of glass. Inside, the air was warm and smelled of damp earth and lemon leaves.

An older woman with silver hair was tying a climbing vine to a wooden frame. When Noah approached, she turned and smiled.

“Mrs. Linden?” he asked.

“Yes, young man. Are you looking for the fern collection?”

Noah held out the postcard first, then the small leather box. “I come from Hale’s Clock Shop. Your postcard arrived this morning, twelve years late.”

Clara’s hand rose to her mouth. She took the postcard and read her own handwriting in silence. Then she opened the leather box and lifted the silver watch by its chain.

“That Saturday,” she said softly, “my sister fell ill in another city. I got on the noon train without stopping at the shop. When I returned months later, I had lost the paper ticket, and I was too shy to ask without it.”

She pressed the watch against her palm. “It belonged to my husband. He was a stationmaster for thirty years.”

Noah handed her the paper bag from the café. “The owner at 14 Station Lane sent this. She says the station clock is still two minutes fast.”

Clara laughed, her eyes bright. She opened the watch cover and listened to its steady tick. “And this one is right on time,” she said. “Thank you for bringing it home.”

note: 适合英语中高级（CEFR B2）读者的悬疑轻科幻：声学研究员在退潮时的海湾接收到一段规律的脉冲信号。
title: Signal at Low Tide
synopsis: At a coastal acoustics station, an ocean researcher records a repeating underwater pulse that only appears during the lowest autumn tide.
bible: Dr. Elena Vance is an ocean acoustics researcher. Marcus is the harbour engineer. Setting: Greyhaven Marine Station. Fair-play mystery grounded in real acoustic science.
outline: Elena detects a precise three-note pulse from the outer bay during low tide.
Elena and Marcus triangulate the sound to an abandoned tidal turbine.
They recover an old oceanographic buoy still transmitting forty years of tide data.
sample: At 04:12, when the tide dropped below the basalt reef, the hydrophone array registered a sequence of three clear pulses. Unlike whale song or harbour engines, the interval between each note was exact to a tenth of a second.
memory: Elena and Marcus recovered the forgotten drift buoy trapped beneath the old turbine pier and preserved its forty-year acoustic log.

preset.preferences: A fair-play coastal mystery with realistic acoustic details and adult researchers.

chapters.title: 1 · Three Notes in the Dark
chapters.summary: Elena records a structured acoustic pulse that appears only when the tide drops below the reef.
chapters.memory: The signal comes from 3200Hz at low water near the northern breakwater.
chapters.text:
At 04:12, when the autumn tide dropped below the basalt reef, the hydrophone array registered a sequence of three clear pulses. Unlike whale song or the low rumble of cargo vessels offshore, the interval between each note was exact to a tenth of a second.

Elena set her mug down and adjusted the spectrogram on her monitor. Three narrow horizontal lines glowed green against the dark background: 3.2 kilohertz, repeated every forty-five seconds.

For three nights she had suspected an instrument fault. Yet when she switched to the backup sensor mounted on the northern breakwater, the same pattern emerged the moment the water level fell below datum.

Why only at low tide? In shallow coastal water, sound travels through a shifting channel bounded by the sea surface and the rocky floor. When the water was deep, waves crashing over the outer reef scattered high-frequency signals. Only when the exposed basalt blocked the open ocean swell did the inner bay become quiet enough—and shallow enough—for the weak signal to reach her receiver.

She printed the waveform and walked down to the pier as dawn greyed the horizon. Marcus, the harbour engineer, was coiling a heavy mooring line beside his launch.

“You are up early, Doctor,” he called out.

Elena showed him the chart. “Something is pinging from the old channel north of the reef, Marcus. And it only wakes up when the water drops.”

chapters.title: 2 · Triangulation
chapters.summary: Using two portable hydrophones, Elena and Marcus trace the sound to the submerged foundations of the 1984 tidal pier.
chapters.memory: The signal originates inside the hollow caisson of the 1984 turbine test pier.
chapters.text:
By late afternoon the next low water was approaching. Marcus steered the work boat slowly past the kelp beds while Elena lowered a portable directional hydrophone over the port side.

“Hold her steady here,” she said, watching the arrival-time delay between the boat sensor and the fixed station on shore. Because sound moves through cold seawater at roughly fifteen hundred metres per second, even a fraction of a second in delay was enough to draw a clean hyperbola across her harbor chart.

“Two hundred metres northeast,” she said, pointing toward a line of weathered concrete pilings that rose from the mist. “Right beside the old turbine foundation.”

Marcus frowned. “The experimental tidal station? They decommissioned that in the nineties. There is no power cable out there anymore.”

They tied the boat to an iron ladder bolted into the concrete caisson. As the tide reached its lowest mark, a narrow archway appeared at the base of the hollow structure. Inside the chamber, sheltered from decades of winter storms, something metallic was bumping gently against the stone wall.

Through her headphones, the three-note chime rang out with startling clarity.

chapters.title: 3 · The Long Watch
chapters.summary: They retrieve a 1998 autonomous drift buoy whose salt-water backup cell was triggered by the low tide.
chapters.memory: Complete: The buoy and its memory core are recovered for the marine archive.
chapters.text:
Marcus shone his lantern into the recess. Wedged between two timber beams floated an anodized aluminum cylinder painted faded yellow, its serial plate encrusted with barnacles.

“It is an autonomous coastal profiler from the 1998 shelf survey,” Elena said, recognizing the flared acoustic transducer at its base. “We thought the last of that batch had drifted out into the Atlantic.”

When they hoisted the cylinder onto the deck, the puzzle of the low-tide timing became clear. The buoy’s main battery had died years ago, but its emergency recovery beacon ran on a magnesium-seawater reserve cell mounted near the upper collar. As long as the buoy was pinned high inside the chamber at high tide, the air pocket kept the upper contacts dry. Only when the tide dropped did the buoy settle onto a lower ledge, dipping the reserve collar into the brine and completing the circuit.

Back in the laboratory that evening, Elena connected a serial adapter to the buoy’s sealed memory module. Line by line, years of temperature and current readings scrolled across her screen—an unbroken record of the bay’s changing seasons, kept safe inside the stone pier until someone finally listened.

note: 适合日语 N4 学习者的海边温情物语，自带重点汉字假名注音（Ruby），讲述海边小图书馆里一封旧信的故事。
title: 海辺の小さな図書館
synopsis: 海の近くの小さな図書館で働く美咲が、返却された古い植物図鑑の中から一通の手紙を見つけ、持ち主を探す物語。
bible: 美咲は大人の図書館員。舞台は静かな海辺の町。丁寧で自然な日本語（JLPT N4目安）。
outline: 美咲は古い植物図鑑に挟まれた手紙を見つける。
駅前の花屋の店主から、昔の常連客の話を聞く。
灯台の下のベンチで手紙の持ち主と出会い、栞を返す。
sample: 海辺の町に、小さな図書館がありました。美咲は毎朝、窓を開けて静かな海を見ました。ある日、返された古い本の中から、白い手紙が一通出てきました。
memory: 美咲は灯台のベンチで佐伯さんに植物図鑑の手紙と押し花の栞を渡し、物語は温かく結ばれた。

preset.preferences: 海辺の町を舞台にした、大人が楽しめる温かい物語。自然で読みやすい日本語。

chapters.title: 1 · 図鑑の中の手紙
chapters.summary: 美咲は返却された植物図鑑から、押し花の栞と手紙を見つける。
chapters.memory: 植物図鑑に青い花の栞と「灯台のベンチで待っています」という手紙があった。
chapters.text:
海辺の町に、小さな図書館がありました。図書館の窓からは、青い海と白い灯台がよく見えました。

美咲はこの図書館で働いています。毎朝九時になると、美咲は窓を開けて、海の風を部屋に入れます。波の音を聞きながら本を並べるのが、美咲の一番好きな時間でした。

金曜日の午後、返却ポストに一冊の古い植物図鑑が入っていました。長い間、誰も借りていなかった本です。美咲がページをひらくと、中から白い封筒と、小さな押し花の栞が落ちました。

封筒には名前が書いてありませんでした。中には短い手紙が入っていました。

「この青い花が咲くころ、また灯台のベンチで会いましょう。図鑑を貸してくれてありがとう。」

手紙の紙は少し黄色くなっていました。美咲は押し花の栞をそっと手に取りました。それは、この町の海岸によく咲く小さな青い花でした。

chapters.title: 2 · 駅前の花屋
chapters.summary: 美咲は駅前の花屋を訪ね、青い花と図鑑を借りていた佐伯さんのことを知る。
chapters.memory: 花屋の店主が、先日町に戻ってきた佐伯さんのことを教えてくれた。
chapters.text:
仕事が終わってから、美咲は駅前の小さな花屋へ行きました。花屋の店主である原田さんは、この町の植物のことを何でも知っています。

「こんばんは、原田さん。この押し花の名前を知っていますか。」

美咲が栞を見せると、原田さんは眼鏡を直して微笑みました。

「ああ、これはハマベノギクだよ。秋になると、灯台の近くの海岸にたくさん咲くんだ。そういえば昨日、久しぶりに佐伯さんが店に来て、同じ花を探していたよ。」

「佐伯さんですか？」

「うん。十年前に仕事の都合で遠くの町へ引っ越したんだけど、今週、この町に戻ってきたそうだ。昔はよく図書館で植物の本を借りていたよ。」

美咲は図鑑の貸出カードを思い出しました。確かに、一番最後の行には『佐伯』という名前が書いてありました。美咲はお礼を言って、夕方の海辺へ向かいました。

chapters.title: 3 · 灯台のベンチ
chapters.summary: 灯台のベンチで佐伯さんに手紙と栞を返し、二人は夕方の海を眺める。
chapters.memory: 完結：手紙と栞は無事に佐伯さんの手元に戻った。
chapters.text:
灯台へ続く坂道を登ると、空がオレンジ色に染まっていました。海からの風が涼しく吹いています。

灯台の下の白いベンチに、グレーのコートを着た女性が一人で座っていました。足元には、小さな青い花が咲いています。

美咲はゆっくり近づいて声をかけました。「あの、佐伯さんでしょうか。図書館の美咲と申します。」

女性は驚いて顔を上げました。「ええ、そうですが……。」

美咲はバッグから白い封筒と押し花の栞を取り出しました。「返却された植物図鑑の中に、これが挟まっていました。大切なお手紙ではないかと思って、お持ちしました。」

佐伯さんは栞を受け取ると、懐かしそうに目を細めました。「まあ、ありがとう。引っ越す前に親友がくれた手紙なの。本に挟んだまま見当たらなくなってしまって、昨日やっと本棚の奥から図鑑を見つけたのよ。」

「お友達にも、もう連絡されましたか？」と美咲が聞くと、佐伯さんは笑顔でうなずきました。

「ええ、明日の午後、このベンチで十年ぶりに会う約束をしたところなの。」

夕日が海に沈み、灯台の明かりが静かにともりました。美咲は温かい気持ちで坂道を降り、明日の朝もまた図書館の窓を開けようと思いました。
